question: Can a projection layer make PINN and DeepONet solutions preserve known first integrals to machine precision during long-time integration?

key_findings.claim: A differentiable projection layer enforces known invariants by mapping each candidate state onto their joint level-set manifold.
key_findings.evidence: The final layer solves a constrained nearest-point problem using simplified Newton iterations; exact initial-condition enforcement fixes the target invariant values and a projection schedule gradually increases iterations during training.

key_findings.claim: Projected networks preserve one or several invariants to double-precision tolerance across the reported ODE examples.
key_findings.evidence: Harmonic oscillator, rigid body, double pendulum, conservative Lorenz, and point-vortex experiments show machine-level energy or multi-integral conservation, whereas standard PINN/DeepONet solutions drift and develop nonphysical trajectories.

key_findings.claim: Exact invariant satisfaction is not itself a guarantee of trajectory accuracy or successful projection.
key_findings.evidence: The method assumes the candidate lies near the correct connected component; early training uses a schedule because distant estimates can project incorrectly, and the chaotic double-pendulum solutions differ despite exact energy conservation.

method.core_idea: Append a constrained projection to a hard-initial-condition PINN or DeepONet so outputs lie exactly on the manifold defined by known first integrals.
method.mechanism: Simplified Newton steps solve a nearest-state constraint at collocation points; the number and weight of projection steps increase during training to avoid unstable projection from poor initial candidates.
assumptions: All relevant first integrals and their differentiable forms are known.
The candidate trajectory stays close to the correct connected component of the invariant manifold.
Pointwise invariant projection is appropriate for the ODE state and numerical precision used.

techniques.role: Sets the exact invariant level through the true initial state.
Maps each network output onto the intersection of conserved level sets.
Introduces constraint iterations gradually as the base solver improves.

evaluations.metric: Trajectory geometry and relative invariant error
evaluations.result: Projected PINNs give closed orbits and preserve one/two invariants to machine precision; vanilla PINNs drift.
evaluations.baseline: Standard hard-constrained PINNs and RK4 reference

evaluations.setting: Double pendulum, conservative Lorenz, and three-vortex DeepONets
evaluations.metric: Long-horizon solution and invariant drift under repeated stepping
evaluations.result: Projected DeepONets preserve up to four integrals over 20-500 steps and avoid several nonphysical drifts.

evaluations.metric: Conservation under fixed architecture and training budget
evaluations.result: Four-layer tanh networks trained for 5,000 epochs use enough Newton steps to reach double-precision conservation.
evaluations.baseline: Same network without the projection layer

limitations: The method requires analytically known first integrals and addresses ODEs, not spatial conservation laws in PDEs.
Projection can select the wrong connected component when the candidate is far from the true manifold.
Experiments do not quantify runtime overhead, trajectory error systematically, or comparison with dedicated geometric integrators.
failure_modes: A candidate far from the manifold makes Newton projection diverge or land on a wrong component.
Redundant, singular, or poorly conditioned invariant gradients destabilize the constraint solve.
A solution can satisfy invariants exactly while accumulating phase or chaotic trajectory error.
reusable_insights: Treat physical invariant error and state-trajectory error as separate evaluation axes.
Hard constraints can be staged during training when enforcing them from random initialization is unstable.
A post-hoc projection can wrap different learned solvers if its domain-of-attraction assumptions are tested.
open_questions: Can learned or approximately known invariants be enforced with calibrated uncertainty?
How does projection compare in accuracy and cost with symplectic, discrete-gradient, and other geometric integrators?
What global or weak-form construction can enforce conservation laws for PDE operator learners?

competitive_landscape.title: Physics Informed Deep Learning (Part I): Data-driven Solutions of Nonlinear Partial Differential Equations
competitive_landscape.difference: Standard PINNs penalize differential-equation residuals but do not guarantee first integrals; the reviewed work adds exact state-manifold projection.

competitive_landscape.title: DeepONet: Learning nonlinear operators for identifying differential equations based on the universal approximation theorem of operators
competitive_landscape.difference: DeepONet learns solution operators across inputs; the reviewed work constrains its outputs during iterative time stepping to preserve known invariants.

competitive_landscape.title: Invariant Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Ordinary Differential Equations
competitive_landscape.difference: Invariant PINNs encode Lie-point symmetries of ODEs; this method directly projects onto arbitrary known first-integral level sets, including multiple invariants, without requiring a Lagrangian symmetry derivation.

novelty_assessment: Reviewer inference: projection methods and PINN/DeepONet solvers are established, and symmetry-constrained neural integrators exist. The contribution is a general differentiable projection schedule for arbitrary ODE first integrals demonstrated across both solution and operator networks.
reviewer_notes: All method, implementation, five example systems, and conclusion pages were checked. Competitor primary records checked 2026-08-23. The paper visually shows invariant/trajectory gains but does not establish a fair cost or convergence comparison with classical geometric solvers.
